title: Mahatma Gandhi and the Mass Phase
tagline: Satyagraha, the early campaigns and the mass movements that made nationalism a people’s cause.

overview.intro: Between 1917 and 1935 the centre of Indian politics moved from the councils and the petitions to the streets, the villages and the picket lines, and the change is inseparable from one man and one method. This chapter sets out Gandhi’s philosophy of satyagraha, truth and non-violence, then follows the campaigns in the order the syllabus asks for — Champaran and Kheda, the Rowlatt agitation, Non-Cooperation and Khilafat, the Salt March and Civil Disobedience, and the constructive programme of the Harijan campaigns and village uplift. The examination skill is to describe each movement in the same four parts: the cause or trigger, the method used, the course of events, and the outcome and significance.

facts.label: The method
facts.value: Satyagraha: truth-force or soul-force, holding to one’s cause without hatred and without violence, and willing to suffer.

facts.label: The first campaigns
facts.value: Champaran in 1917 for the indigo cultivators of Bihar, and Kheda in 1918 for the peasants of Gujarat.

facts.label: Non-Cooperation
facts.value: 1920 to 1922: boycott of titles, schools, courts, councils and foreign cloth, withdrawn after Chauri Chaura.

facts.label: The Salt March
facts.value: The march to Dandi in March to April 1930, breaking the salt law and launching Civil Disobedience with the Dharasana raid as its test case.

learningOutcomes: Explain satyagraha, truth and non-violence with reference to Gandhi’s own definitions.
Describe the Champaran and Kheda campaigns and state what they achieved for the cultivators.
Account for the Non-Cooperation and Khilafat movements, their programme and their withdrawal.
Explain the Salt March and Civil Disobedience, including why salt made the ideal mass issue.
Describe the constructive programme, the Harijan campaign and village uplift, and assess Gandhi’s contribution.

blocks.text: Satyagraha literally means holding on to truth, and Gandhi developed it out of his experience of racial discrimination in South Africa, where he found that neither petitions nor retaliatory anger could secure justice for the Indian community. Its premises are three. Truth is God, so the satyagrahi is devoted to truth rather than to victory and is willing to be proved wrong. Non-violence is not weakness but the strongest form of action available to a just cause, since it refuses to dehumanise the opponent and therefore leaves open the possibility of the opponent’s conversion, which violence forecloses for generations. Suffering is the instrument: the satyagrahi courts arrest, accepts blows and endures imprisonment, and by refusing to inflict suffering in turn exposes the injustice of the power that inflicts it. From these premises come the discipline of satyagraha — no hatred of the adversary, no harm to person or property, willingness to negotiate, absolute cleanliness of means and ends, and the readiness to withdraw a movement when the opponent loses the capacity to negotiate fairly, which is precisely the reasoning Gandhi gave when he withdrew Non-Cooperation after Chauri Chaura.

items: Truth first: the satyagrahi seeks the truth rather than victory and accepts correction, so the means must be as clean as the ends.
Non-violence as soul-force: it refuses to injure the opponent and keeps the door open for the opponent’s conversion.
Suffering as method: arrest, blows and imprisonment endured without retaliation are the pressure a satyagrahi applies.
Discipline: no hatred, no destruction of property and no intimidation of the opponent’s supporters.
Self-criticism and self-reliance: spinning, fasting, cleanliness and the constructive programme are part of the same method.
Capacity to withdraw: a movement is suspended when the conditions for non-violent negotiation cease to hold.

blocks.caption: Satyagraha and ordinary political pressure
rows: To reach truth and convert the opponent
Negotiation or withdrawal when fairness fails

items.note: Gandhi’s fasts were never threats to a person but appeals to the adversary’s conscience, which is why they were directed at his own side in 1924 as often as at the government in 1943.
The protest was to be non-violent in the strictest sense, and Gandhi withdrew the movement when he received reports of violence, because a movement that turns violent loses its claim to truth.

items.meaning: Truth-force: the method of resisting injustice without hatred or violence and by being willing to suffer.
Non-injury in thought, word and deed, the foundation on which satyagraha rests.
The use of what is produced in one’s own country, expressed in Gandhi’s programme through spinning and khadi.
The welfare of all, the label Gandhi gave to the constructive programme and the uplift of the weakest.

learn.title: Champaran and Kheda: the first campaigns in India

blocks.text: Gandhi returned to India in 1915 and, on the advice of Gokhale, spent his first year travelling and observing rather than speaking, which is why his first Indian campaigns began only in 1917. Champaran in Bihar concerned the indigo cultivators of the Tinkathia system, under which they were compelled to grow indigo on three twentieths of their land for the planter at a ruinous price and were loaded with illegal dues; Gandhi was invited by Raj Kumar Shukla, travelled there, was ordered to leave by the district magistrate, refused to go and accepted the consequences, and the government was forced to appoint an inquiry committee on which Gandhi served, leading to the abolition of the system and the return of illegal dues. Kheda in Gujarat in 1918 concerned peasants whose crops had failed but who were still being pressed for the full land revenue; Gandhi advised them to pay the revenue they could afford and to withhold the rest while presenting their case, and the government eventually suspended the revenue demand for the year and remitted the arrears of the poorest. Both campaigns established his method in India: enter the locality, understand the grievance from the people themselves, demand what is legally right, suffer the consequences and let the moral pressure force a negotiation.

items: Champaran, 1917: the indigo Tinkathia system of Bihar; invited by Raj Kumar Shukla; refusal to obey an order to leave; official inquiry and abolition of the system.
Kheda, 1918: revenue suspension after crop failure, with peasants asked to pay what they could and resist the rest non-violently.
Both were local, concrete and legal, which is why they won practical relief rather than promises.
Both demonstrated satyagraha on Indian soil and gave Gandhi the credibility that a mass movement required.
The method in each: study the grievance, organise the people, ask for the lawful remedy, accept the penalty.

blocks.caption: Champaran and Kheda compared
rows: Forced indigo cultivation and illegal dues
Inquiry and abolition of the system
Suspension of demand and waiver for the poor

items.note: A cultivator who insisted that Gandhi visit Champaran and would not take no for an answer, which is how a local grievance reached a national leader.
By advising the Kheda peasants to pay what they could, Gandhi kept the campaign lawful and denied the government the argument that the peasants were simply refusing to pay.

learn.title: The Rowlatt agitation and Non-Cooperation with Khilafat

blocks.text: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 kept in force the wartime repressive provisions, allowing detention without trial and trial without jury, and it was passed despite the unanimous opposition of the Indian members of the Imperial Legislative Council. Gandhi called it a permanent infamy, launched a nationwide hartal and fast, and when the movement showed signs of disorder withdrew it — but not before the protests at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar on 13 April 1919, where General Dyer ordered firing on a peaceful gathering enclosed in a walled ground, killing hundreds. The Non-Cooperation movement of 1920 to 1922 was Gandhi’s answer to the combination of the Rowlatt Act, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the Khilafat grievance: the Congress at the special Calcutta session of September 1920 and at Nagpur in December 1920 adopted a programme of the surrender of titles and honours, the boycott of schools, colleges, courts, councils, the army and police, the boycott of foreign cloth, and the adoption of khadi, national schools, national councils and panchayats. The Khilafat Committee, led by the Ali brothers, joined the movement so that Hindus and Muslims campaigned together for the first time. The movement brought millions into politics and was withdrawn in February 1922 after the Chauri Chaura incident, where a crowd burned a police station killing twenty-two policemen, and Gandhi suspended the campaign even against the wishes of many Congress leaders because he judged that the country was not yet disciplined enough for non-violence.

items: Rowlatt Act, 1919: detention without trial and trial without jury; Gandhi called a hartal and fast and then withdrew the agitation when disorder appeared.
Jallianwala Bagh, 13 April 1919: General Dyer fired on an enclosed peaceful gathering; the Hunter Committee later censured him while the House of Lords praised him.
Non-Cooperation, 1920 to 1922: surrender of titles, boycott of schools, courts, councils, foreign cloth and the services, with national alternatives.
Khilafat: the Ali brothers and the Khilafat Committee joined, creating Hindu-Muslim unity in a single mass movement.
Withdrawal on 5 February 1922 after the Chauri Chaura arson, on Gandhi’s insistence that means must be as clean as ends.
Consequences: mass participation, the growth of the Congress as a mass organisation, and the durability of khadi as a symbol.

blocks.caption: The Non-Cooperation programme
rows: The pride of refusing British distinctions
Panchayats and arbitration by Indian members
Petition and public agitation outside them
The army, police and government service
Service to the national cause through the Congress

items.note: Gandhi regarded the burning of the police station as a failure of the movement rather than an act of it, and he suspended a campaign at its height on that principle.
Wearing khadi made a political statement in an ordinary act of dressing, which is why the boycott of foreign cloth reached households that had never attended a meeting.

learn.title: The Salt March and Civil Disobedience

blocks.text: By 1930 the political situation was strained by the Simon Commission, which arrived in 1927 with no Indian member and was met with black flags and the slogan Simon Go Back, by the rejection of the Nehru Report by the Muslim League, and by the failure of the constitutional conferences to produce an advance. Gandhi chose salt with a strategist’s instinct: every household used it, the tax fell on the poorest, and the monopoly was a symbol of a government that taxed even the need to eat. On 12 March 1930 he walked from the Sabarmati Ashram with seventy-eight followers, and on 6 April at Dandi he picked up a handful of natural salt, breaking the salt law; within weeks salt was being made and sold illegally across the country and the movement spread to the Punjab, the North-West Frontier Province under Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan’s Red Shirts, and Bengal. The government arrested some sixty thousand people, and when the movement continued, the raid on the Dharasana salt works on 21 May 1930 became the test case: row after row of volunteers walked into the lathis without raising an arm, and the reports filed by Webb Miller and carried in world newspapers did more damage to British claims of civilised rule than any violence could have done. Gandhi was arrested in May 1930 and released in January 1931 to attend the conference in London, where he argued that independence was the only remedy, and the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931 followed, with the Congress agreeing to suspend Civil Disobedience and the government releasing political prisoners and allowing the making of salt for personal use.

items: The trigger: the Simon Commission of 1927 with no Indian member, the failure of constitutional talks and the general political deadlock.
The issue: the salt monopoly and tax, chosen because it affected every household and the poorest most of all.
The march: 12 March 1930 from Sabarmati with seventy-eight followers; the salt law broken at Dandi on 6 April 1930.
The spread: illegal salt-making everywhere, and extension to the Frontier under Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan and to Bengal and the Punjab.
The test case: the Dharasana raid of 21 May 1930, non-violent volunteers advancing into lathis without resistance and reported worldwide.
The outcome: mass arrests, the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931, the conference in London and the suspension of the movement.

blocks.caption: Salt as the centre of a movement
rows: Every household used it and could therefore join in an ordinary act
The tax bore hardest on the poorest, so the grievance was self-evident
It showed a government taxing even the necessities of life
Making and taking salt needed no organisation, no funds and no leader
Breaking a bad law non-violently expressed satyagraha perfectly

items.note: Volunteers formed lines and walked forward until struck down, while the next line stepped up, and not one of them raised a hand in defence — the discipline satyagraha demanded.
Families boiling brine in their courtyards turned a law into a dead letter in weeks, which is why the government could not arrest its way out of the movement.

learn.title: The constructive programme: Harijan uplift and village work

blocks.text: Gandhi always regarded the constructive programme as the other half of politics, and after the Salt March he turned to it with particular energy. Against untouchability he began a fast in September 1932 against the Communal Award, which had proposed separate electorates for the Depressed Classes, and the resulting Poona Pact between him and Dr Ambedkar replaced separate electorates with reserved seats and a joint electorate. He then took the name Harijan, the people of God, for the outcast communities, travelled through their villages, opened temples to them, founded the Harijan Sevak Sangh in 1933 and published Harijan as a weekly, and made the removal of untouchability a condition of India’s own freedom, arguing that a country that treats a section of its people as polluting cannot be said to be free even after the British leave. Alongside this went village work: khadi and spinning as a means of giving the village its own cloth and its own leisure-time employment, village sanitation, basic education, harmony between Hindus, Muslims, Christians and Parsis, and the promotion of Hindi as a national language. These were not diversions from politics but the training ground in which ordinary Indians learned to take responsibility for their own affairs, which is what Gandhi meant by swaraj in the individual and in the nation at once.

items: Harijan uplift: the fast of 1932, the Poona Pact with Dr Ambedkar, the Harijan Sevak Sangh of 1933 and the weekly Harijan.
Opening of temples and wells to the Depressed Classes and the preaching of the removal of untouchability as a religious duty.
Village work: spinning and khadi for cloth and employment, sanitation, basic education and village industries.
Harmony between communities and the development of Hindi as a national language linking the north and the south.
The constructive programme as political training: swaraj in the individual through self-discipline, and in the nation through self-reliance.
The judgement: without the removal of untouchability, Gandhi argued, political freedom would remain incomplete.

items.note: The agreement with Dr Ambedkar replaced separate electorates for the Depressed Classes with reserved seats in a joint electorate, which Gandhi preferred on the ground that separate electorates would divide Hindus permanently.

items.text: A spinning wheel in every household
items.note: Gandhi made charkha spinning a daily discipline to give villages their own cloth, to use idle hours and to make economic independence a habit rather than a slogan.

items.meaning: The name Gandhi gave to the outcast communities, meaning people of God, and used for the campaign against untouchability.
The 1932 agreement between Gandhi and Dr Ambedkar substituting reserved seats in a joint electorate for separate electorates.
Hand-spun and hand-woven cloth, the material symbol of swadeshi and of village self-reliance.
The body of social work — sanitation, spinning, education, harmony and the removal of untouchability — that Gandhi treated as part of the freedom struggle.

learn.title: Assessing Gandhi’s contribution to the freedom movement

blocks.text: The assessment question should be answered by naming what changed because of Gandhi rather than by praise. First, he made nationalism a mass movement: Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience brought peasants, workers, women and students into politics in numbers no earlier leader had reached, and the khadi-clad village volunteer became the image of the movement. Second, he changed the method of politics by making non-violent mass action a disciplined technique rather than a sentiment, with rules, negotiation, suspension and a willingness to be arrested. Third, he connected the political demand to social reform: untouchability, village industry, Hindu-Muslim harmony and the dignity of women were treated as preconditions of freedom rather than as matters to be settled afterwards. Fourth, he gave the movement a moral claim on the world, so that the British had to justify their rule against a leadership that refused to strike back, as the Dharasana reports made plain. The limitations should be stated with equal honesty: the movements were suspended at their height, the programme of non-cooperation rested on a discipline that could fail at any moment as Chauri Chaura showed, the economic programme of spinning could not by itself solve industrial poverty, and the relationship with Dr Ambedkar over separate electorates left a difficult legacy. The balanced verdict is that Gandhi supplied the freedom movement with both a goal that the ordinary Indian could feel and a method ordinary Indians could practise.

items: Mass base: peasants, workers, women and students entered politics through Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience.
Method: non-violence became a disciplined technique with rules, suspension and negotiation rather than a moral ideal alone.
Social fusion: freedom was made to include the removal of untouchability, village self-reliance and communal harmony.
Moral authority: a leadership that refused to hit back made British rule harder to defend before the world.
Limitations: movements withdrawn at their height, discipline that could break as at Chauri Chaura, and a contested legacy on separate electorates.
Verdict: he gave the movement a goal the ordinary Indian could feel and a method the ordinary Indian could practise.

items.note: Three achievements with instances, two limitations with instances, then a one-sentence verdict that says what changed in Indian politics.
Its economic purpose, its political symbolism, its role in the boycott of foreign cloth and its place in the constructive programme.

examFocus: Movement questions follow the same four parts: cause or trigger, method, course, outcome and significance.
Always give the dates: 1917 Champaran, 1918 Kheda, 1919 Rowlatt and Amritsar, 1920 to 1922 Non-Cooperation, 6 April 1930 Dandi.
Explain why a chosen issue worked — salt because it was universal, cheap, symbolic and simple.
The withdrawal questions expect the reasoning, not just the fact: means must be as clean as ends.
Assessment answers need achievements, limitations and a closing verdict, each with an instance.

questions.explanation: The agreement with Dr Ambedkar replaced separate electorates for the Depressed Classes with reserved seats in a joint electorate.

questions.prompt: The method of non-violent resistance based on truth developed by Gandhi is called __________.
questions.explanation: Satyagraha literally means holding on to truth and was developed by Gandhi in South Africa.

questions.explanation: Shaukat Ali and Muhammad Ali led the Khilafat agitation, which joined Non-Cooperation to create Hindu-Muslim unity.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by satyagraha and state its essential features.
questions.answer: Satyagraha means holding on to truth: the satyagrahi seeks justice by appealing to the conscience of the adversary rather than by coercing him. Its essential features are strict non-violence in thought, word and deed; a willingness to suffer arrest, blows and imprisonment without retaliating; respect for the adversary and the absence of hatred; means as clean as ends; and the discipline to suspend a movement when the conditions for non-violent negotiation fail.
questions.explanation: Truth-seeking, non-violence, willingness to suffer, respect for the opponent and clean means are the features to list.

questions.prompt: Why did Gandhi choose salt as the issue for the Civil Disobedience Movement?
questions.answer: Salt was chosen because it was universal — every household used it and could therefore join in an ordinary act — and because the tax bore hardest on the poorest, so the injustice was self-evident to everyone. The salt monopoly also symbolised a government that taxed even a necessity of life, and making or taking salt required no organisation, no funds and no leader, which meant a village could act on its own. Breaking a bad law non-violently was also a perfect expression of satyagraha, since the punishment could be accepted openly.
questions.explanation: Universality, its burden on the poor, its symbolism, the ease of defiance and its fit with satyagraha are the five reasons.

questions.prompt: State two measures Gandhi took against untouchability.
questions.answer: He undertook a fast in 1932 against the Communal Award’s separate electorates for the Depressed Classes, which resulted in the Poona Pact with Dr Ambedkar providing reserved seats in a joint electorate. He also founded the Harijan Sevak Sangh in 1933, published the weekly Harijan, travelled among the outcast communities, and campaigned to open temples and wells to them.
questions.explanation: Any two of the fast and Poona Pact, the Harijan Sevak Sangh, the journal Harijan, and the opening of temples and wells.

questions.prompt: Describe the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920 to 1922, giving its causes, its programme and the reason for its withdrawal.
questions.answer: The causes were a combination of grievances: the Rowlatt Act of 1919, which permitted detention without trial; the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 13 April 1919, which showed the brutality of the regime and was followed by the reward rather than the punishment of General Dyer; the disappointment with the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms as inadequate; and the Khilafat grievance of Indian Muslims over the peace settlement of the First World War. The programme adopted at the Calcutta session of September 1920 and confirmed at Nagpur in December 1920 comprised the surrender of titles and honours, the boycott of government schools and colleges, law courts, councils, the army and police, and the boycott of foreign cloth in favour of khadi, together with the creation of national schools, national councils and panchayats as alternatives. Millions joined, women and students prominently, and the Khilafat leadership made it the first sustained Hindu-Muslim campaign together. The movement was withdrawn on 5 February 1922 after a crowd at Chauri Chaura burned a police station killing twenty-two policemen, because Gandhi held that a mass movement must be as pure in its means as in its ends and that the country had not yet been trained in disciplined non-violence.
questions.explanation: Causes with the grievous events, the full programme with its alternatives, and the withdrawal explained by the doctrine of means.

questions.prompt: Assess Gandhi’s contribution to the Indian freedom movement, stating both achievements and limitations.
questions.answer: Achievements: first, he transformed the Congress from a forum of the educated into a mass movement, since Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience drew peasants, workers, women and students into politics in numbers no earlier campaign had reached. Second, he converted non-violence from a moral ideal into a workable political technique, with clear rules, organisation, negotiation and suspension, so that a subject people could act against an armed government without arms. Third, he fused social reform with political freedom, making the removal of untouchability, village self-reliance through khadi, communal harmony and the dignity of women part of the meaning of swaraj rather than matters to be postponed until after independence. Fourth, he gave the movement a moral authority before the world, as the disciplined lines at Dharasana demonstrated to international opinion. Limitations: the mass campaigns were suspended at their height, in 1922 and again during Civil Disobedience, so gains were often surrendered before they could be consolidated; the discipline on which non-violence depended could break locally, as Chauri Chaura showed; the constructive programme of spinning could not answer industrial poverty on its own; and his position against separate electorates in the Poona Pact remained contested by Dr Ambedkar and others. The verdict is that Gandhi gave the movement both a goal the ordinary Indian could feel in daily life and a method the ordinary Indian could practise without arms.
questions.explanation: Four achievements and four limitations each with an instance, closed by a verdict on goal and method.

questions.prompt: Compare the Salt March campaign with Non-Cooperation as means of mass mobilisation, and explain why salt succeeded where a general boycott had limits.
questions.answer: Both used boycott and the acceptance of arrest, but they differed in entry point. Non-Cooperation asked people to give up institutions — schools, courts, councils and titles — which required a decision that was easier for the educated and the professional to take, and its alternative institutions needed organisation and money, so participation depended on having something to substitute. Civil Disobedience began with an act that everyone could perform: making or taking salt needed no substitute, no funds and no organisation, so a cultivator with no schooling could join on the same day as a lawyer, and the grievance itself — a tax on a necessity — was immediately intelligible. Salt also had a symbolic precision that foreign cloth lacked, since it showed a government that taxed even the act of eating, and the breaking of a law by ordinary people made the repression visible, as the Dharasana reports proved. Non-Cooperation therefore built the machinery of the movement while salt brought in the masses who could not use that machinery, which is why the two campaigns together, rather than either alone, made nationalism a people’s cause.
questions.explanation: The comparison must contrast the entry point, the resources participation required and the visibility of repression that each campaign produced.
